name: Acid body wash (AHA/BHA) for pits

lead: Users lather acid washes onto the armpits hoping for fresher-smelling underarms and smoother skin.

AHAs such as glycolic or lactic acid, or BHA (salicylic acid), chemically exfoliate by loosening dead skin cells. Proponents say removing dead skin and lowering surface pH makes life harder for odor-causing bacteria. Acid washes are well known as exfoliants, and no studies of them for underarm odor were found.

paras: Used in the shower in place of or alongside regular body wash on the underarms, a few times a week, and followed by deodorant.
Reported effects are mild irritation, redness and flaking, and the FDA cautions that these products can raise sunburn likelihood.

chain: Acid exfoliates and lowers skin pH
angle.text: Users apply AHA or BHA washes to the armpits on the idea that exfoliation and lower pH make life harder for odor bacteria. The acids are established exfoliants; no studies have looked at underarm odor.

lead: Acid body washes contain alpha hydroxy acids (AHAs) such as glycolic, lactic or mandelic acid, or the beta hydroxy acid (BHA) salicylic acid, which chemically exfoliate skin.[1][2] In looksmaxxing and grooming discussions they are used on the armpits with the aim of reducing underarm odor and keeping the skin smooth, on the theory that removing dead skin and lowering skin pH leaves less for odor-causing bacteria to work on.

Wikipedia's body odor article says underarm smell mainly comes from bacteria such as Corynebacterium and Staphylococcus breaking down apocrine sweat, and that listed treatments include antibacterial soap, deodorants, antiperspirants and aluminum chloride; it does not mention acid exfoliants.[3] Salicylic acid is described as a keratolytic used for acne, calluses, keratosis pilaris and acanthosis nigricans, among other conditions, and glycolic acid is used in many skin-care products.[2][4]
No study of acid washes for underarm odor was found.
infobox: FDA cautions AHAs can raise sunburn likelihood[1]

paras: AHAs such as glycolic, lactic, mandelic and citric acid are used in cosmetics for chemical exfoliation, and BHAs differ structurally in that their functional groups are separated by two carbon atoms.[1] Salicylic acid removes the outermost skin layer and is oil-soluble, which Wikipedia associates with keeping pores from clogging.[2] EU cosmetic rules cap salicylic acid at 3 percent in rinse-off hair products and 2 percent in other products.[2]

Proponents say acidic exfoliation reduces the bacteria that produce armpit odor. The body odor article describes how Corynebacterium lipases break sweat lipids into odorous molecules and notes that genetics, such as the ABCC11 gene variant, also influence armpit smell.[3] Its listed prevention methods include daily washing with antibacterial soap and applying deodorant or antiperspirant.[3]

When used as directed, AHAs are generally considered safe, and the FDA and the Cosmetic Ingredient Review panel consider them safe at low concentrations, at pH above 3.5, with clear safety instructions.[1] The FDA has cautioned that AHAs can increase the likelihood of sunburn, an effect reversible when use stops.[1] Glycolic acid is described as a skin irritant, and salicylic acid causes mild skin irritation, with toxicity reported mainly from oral overdose or large-area high-concentration application.[2][4]
